sk: पुरमेकादशद्वारमजस्यावक्रचेतसः | अनुष्ठाय न शोचति विमुक्तश्च विमुच्यते | एतद्वै तत् ||
ro: puram · ekādaśa-dvāram · ajasya · avakra-cetasaḥ | anuṣṭhāya · na · śocati · vimuktaḥ · ca · vimucyate | etat · vai · tat ||
hi: अज (अजन्मा परमात्मा) की — जिसकी चेतना सरल (ऋजु, वक्र-रहित) है — एकादश-द्वार (ग्यारह द्वारों) वाली पुरी (नगरी/शरीर) का ध्यान करके साधक शोक नहीं करता; वह विमुक्त होता है और पूर्णतः मुक्त हो जाता है। यही वह (ब्रह्म) है।
en: The city of the unborn (Self), whose consciousness is free from crookedness, has eleven gates. By meditating upon it, one grieves no more; one is liberated and is fully set free. This, verily, is That.

ws.e: city — the body as a fortified city; cognate with Greek polis; the body is a dwelling-place of the Self
having eleven gates — the eleven openings of the body: 2 eyes, 2 ears, 2 nostrils, mouth, navel, crown (brahma-randhra), and 2 lower apertures
of the unborn — aja: a (not) + ja (born); the Self that was never born and never dies
whose consciousness is not crooked — avakra (straight, uncurved) + cetas (mind/consciousness); the Self's awareness is direct and undistorted
having meditated upon — absolutive of anu + √sthā; by contemplating, by taking one's stand in
liberated — freed from bondage; past participle of vi + √muc
is fully released — passive present; the repetition (vimuktaḥ ca vimucyate) emphasises complete and irreversible liberation

gr: puram ekādaśa-dvāram — 'city with eleven gates': the body conceived as a fortified city with eleven openings. This image recurs in the Bhagavad Gītā (5.13). ajasya avakra-cetasaḥ — genitive: 'of the unborn whose consciousness is straight'; the city belongs to the Self, not the other way around. vimuktaḥ ca vimucyate — emphatic doubling: 'liberated, he is set free' — liberation is both a state and an ongoing release. etat vai tat — 'this verily is That': the refrain linking each teaching back to the ultimate reality Nachiketa seeks.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_2.1.1 — This verse opens Adhyaya 2 with the famous 'city of eleven gates' metaphor. The Bhagavad Gītā (5.13) echoes this directly: 'sarva-karmāṇi manasā sannyasyāste sukhaṁ vaśī, nava-dvāre pure dehī' — there Kṛṣṇa says 'nine gates' (counting only the visible openings), while the Upanishad counts eleven (adding brahma-randhra and navel).

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'पुर' शरीर है और 'अज' आत्मा है जो इसमें निवास करता है — जैसे राजा नगर में रहता है पर नगर उसे बाँधता नहीं। आत्मा शरीर का स्वामी है, दास नहीं। ग्यारह द्वारों का ध्यान यह बोध कराता है कि शरीर एक यन्त्र है, 'मैं' नहीं।
advaita.en: Shankara says the 'city' is the body and the 'unborn' is the Self dwelling in it — as a king lives in a city without being bound by it. The Self is the master of the body, not its servant. Meditating on the eleven gates reveals that the body is an instrument, not the 'I'.
advaita.ins: You are not the house — you are the one who lives in it. Know the gates for what they are: openings in a temporary structure, not your identity.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि शरीर-रूपी नगरी भगवान् (अन्तर्यामी) की है — वे इसमें निवास करते हैं और इसे नियन्त्रित करते हैं। जीवात्मा भी इसी नगरी में रहता है, पर भगवान् की अधीनता में। 'अनुष्ठाय' — भगवान् की उपासना करके ही मुक्ति होती है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the body-city belongs to the Lord (the inner controller) — He dwells in it and governs it. The jīvātman also resides in this city, but under the Lord's sovereignty. 'Anuṣṭhāya' — liberation comes only through worship of the Lord.
vishisht.ins: The body is a temple of the Lord, not just a mechanical structure. Every gate is an entry point for divine service — each sense can be turned toward God.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द शरीर को चेतना का एक संगठित यन्त्र (organised instrument) मानते हैं — ग्यारह द्वार ग्यारह प्रकार की चेतना-गतिविधि हैं। 'अवक्रचेतस्' — आत्मा की चेतना सीधी (direct) है; मन की तरह वक्र नहीं।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo sees the body as an organised instrument of consciousness — the eleven gates are eleven modes of conscious activity. 'Avakra-cetas' — the Self's consciousness is direct, not curved and refracting like the mind.
aurobindo.ins: The mind distorts reality by bending it through desire and fear. The Self sees straight — without refraction. Meditation aligns the mental lens with the direct light of the Self.

dp.q: 🔍 What are the eleven gates of the body-city?
dp.a: The ekādaśa-dvāra (eleven gates) are the eleven openings of the human body through which consciousness interacts with the external world. The standard enumeration is: (1-2) two eyes — gates of sight; (3-4) two ears — gates of hearing; (5-6) two nostrils — gates of smell and breath; (7) mouth — gate of speech, taste, and food; (8) navel — gate of vital energy (prāṇa distribution); (9) brahma-randhra (crown aperture) — gate through which the soul departs at death; (10-11) two lower apertures — gates of excretion and reproduction. The Bhagavad Gītā (5.13) uses a slightly different count of nine gates (nava-dvāra), omitting the navel and brahma-randhra. The metaphor conveys that the Self dwells within this city but is not identical with it — like a king who rules from within the city walls but whose identity is not the walls themselves.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does liberation require 'no grief' (na śocati)?
dp.a: The phrase na śocati (does not grieve) points to grief as the hallmark of bondage. The Upanishads consistently identify grief (śoka) with ignorance — the failure to recognise one's true nature as the deathless Self. In the Chāndogya Upanishad (7.1.3), Nārada says to Sanatkumāra: 'śrutaṁ hy eva me bhagavad-dṛśebhyaḥ, tarati śokam ātmavit' — 'I have heard from teachers like you that the knower of the Self crosses beyond grief.' And the Mundaka (2.2.8) declares: 'bhidyate hṛdaya-granthiḥ, chidyante sarva-saṁśayāḥ' — 'the knot of the heart is cut, all doubts are destroyed.' Grief arises from identification with what is perishable — body, relationships, possessions. When one meditates on the body as merely a 'city' inhabited by the eternal Self, the cause of grief dissolves. The Self was never born, never dies, and never loses anything — so what is there to grieve?

sk: हंसः शुचिषद्वसुरन्तरिक्षसद्धोता वेदिषदतिथिर्दुरोणसत् | नृषद्वरसदृतसद्व्योमसदब्जा गोजा ऋतजा अद्रिजा ऋतं बृहत् ||
ro: haṁsaḥ · śuciṣat · vasuḥ · antarikṣa-sat · hotā · vediṣat · atithiḥ · duroṇa-sat | nṛṣat · vara-sat · ṛta-sat · vyoma-sat · abjāḥ · gojāḥ · ṛtajāḥ · adrijāḥ · ṛtaṁ · bṛhat ||
hi: वह (आत्मा) हंस (सूर्य) है, शुचि (अग्नि/प्रकाश) में स्थित; वसु (वायु) है, अन्तरिक्ष में स्थित; होता (पुरोहित) है, वेदी पर स्थित; अतिथि है, गृह में स्थित; मनुष्यों में स्थित, श्रेष्ठ में स्थित, ऋत (सत्य) में स्थित, आकाश (व्योम) में स्थित — जल से उत्पन्न, किरणों से उत्पन्न, ऋत (सत्य) से उत्पन्न, पर्वतों से उत्पन्न — वह विराट ऋत (कॉस्मिक ऑर्डर) है।
en: He is the sun (haṁsa) dwelling in the bright sky; the wind (vasu) dwelling in the mid-region; the priest (hotā) seated at the altar; the guest seated in the house; dwelling among men, in the noble, in cosmic order, in space — born of water, born of light, born of truth, born of rock — He is the great cosmic Truth (ṛtam bṛhat).

ws.e: the swan/sun — haṁsa literally means 'swan' but denotes the sun moving across the sky; also the Self that 'migrates' through states of consciousness
dwelling in the bright — śuci (pure/bright, i.e., the sky of light) + sat (dwelling); the sun's station
vasu — wind; one of the eight Vasus (elemental deities), here meaning the wind as life-breath of the cosmos
the invoking priest — hotṛ, the chief priest who recites mantras at the altar
the guest — atithi (without a fixed date, hence 'guest'); the sacred fire is the perpetual guest in every household
the great Truth — ṛta (cosmic order) + bṛhat (vast/great); the all-pervading principle of order

gr: haṁsaḥ — 'swan/sun': the word haṁsa has a profound double meaning — it is both the sun that 'migrates' across the sky and the Self (so'ham = sa + aham = 'I am He' reversed as haṁ-sa). The eight epithets (śuciṣat, antarikṣa-sat, etc.) show that the Self pervades every level of existence: sky, mid-region, ritual altar, home, humanity, cosmic law, and space. abjāḥ gojāḥ ṛtajāḥ adrijāḥ — four 'births' or origins: water, light-rays, truth, and mountains — showing the Self as the source of all elements. ṛtaṁ bṛhat — the climactic declaration: the Self IS the vast cosmic order itself.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_2.1.2 — This verse is identical to Rig Veda 4.40.5 and also appears in the Vājasaneyi Saṁhitā. It is one of the most celebrated cosmic hymns, showing the One Self pervading all forms and functions — sun, wind, fire, priest, guest, truth. The identification of ātman with ṛtaṁ bṛhat is the Upanishad's way of saying: the Self is not just a personal principle but the cosmic order itself.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि यह मन्त्र ब्रह्म की सर्वव्यापकता (omnipresence) दिखाता है — वही सूर्य है, वायु है, अग्नि है, अतिथि है। जो विभिन्न नाम-रूपों में भिन्न प्रतीत होता है, वह एक ही अद्वैत ब्रह्म है। 'ऋतं बृहत्' — ब्रह्म ही विराट सत्य है।
advaita.en: Shankara says this mantra demonstrates Brahman's omnipresence — it is the sun, the wind, the fire, the guest. What appears different under various names and forms is one non-dual Brahman. 'Ṛtaṁ bṛhat' — Brahman is the vast Truth.
advaita.ins: Look at the sun — you see Brahman in the sky. Feel the wind — you feel Brahman in the air. Light a fire — Brahman sits at your hearth. There is nowhere Brahman is not.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि भगवान् ही सूर्य में, वायु में, अग्नि में, और सर्वत्र अन्तर्यामी रूप से व्याप्त हैं। वे प्रत्येक वस्तु की अन्तरात्मा हैं — सूर्य भगवान् की देह है, वायु भगवान् की देह है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the Lord pervades everything as the inner controller — in the sun, in the wind, in fire, everywhere. Each entity is the Lord's body — the sun is His body, the wind is His body.
vishisht.ins: The universe is not separate from God — it is His body, animated by His presence. To worship the sun is to worship its indwelling Lord.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द इसमें एक चेतना (One Consciousness) का विस्तार देखते हैं — जो सूर्य के रूप में प्रकाशित होती है, वायु के रूप में गतिशील होती है, अग्नि के रूप में रूपान्तरित करती है। 'ऋतं बृहत्' — यह चेतना ही कॉस्मिक ऑर्डर है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo sees in this the expansion of One Consciousness — which illuminates as the sun, moves as the wind, transforms as fire. 'Ṛtaṁ bṛhat' — this consciousness IS the cosmic order.
aurobindo.ins: The Vedic seers did not see dead matter animated by a distant God — they saw consciousness expressing itself as every force and form in the universe.

dp.q: 🔍 What is the significance of the word 'haṁsa'?
dp.a: The word haṁsa is one of the most layered terms in Sanskrit. On the surface it means 'swan' — the bird that migrates across great distances. By extension it means the sun, which 'migrates' across the sky daily. But the deepest meaning is esoteric: haṁsa = haṁ + sa = 'I am He', a reversal of the mahāvākya so'ham (sa + aham = 'He am I'). With every breath, the scriptures say, the jīva unconsciously chants 'haṁ-sa, haṁ-sa' — the inhalation sounds 'haṁ' and the exhalation 'sa.' The paramahaṁsa (supreme swan) is one who has realised this identity consciously. The swan also has the legendary ability to separate milk from water (viveka) — hence haṁsa symbolises discriminative wisdom. In this Katha verse, haṁsa refers primarily to the sun — the visible symbol of the Self's light pervading the cosmos.

dp.q: 🔍 How does this verse connect the ritual and the cosmic?
dp.a: This verse is remarkable because it bridges the Vedic ritual world and the Upanishadic cosmic vision in a single breath. The eight 'dwelling-places' form an ascending scale: (1) śuciṣat — in the bright sky (physical cosmos); (2) antarikṣa-sat — in the mid-region (atmospheric); (3) vediṣat — at the ritual altar (sacred ritual); (4) duroṇa-sat — in the home (domestic life); (5) nṛṣat — among men (social); (6) vara-sat — in the noble/excellent (ethical); (7) ṛta-sat — in cosmic order (metaphysical); (8) vyoma-sat — in space (absolute). The message is that the Self is not only the transcendent reality beyond the world — it is equally the immanent presence within every level of existence, from the humblest home to the vastest space. The four 'births' (water, light, truth, rock) reinforce this: the Self is the origin of every element, not just the 'spiritual' ones.

sk: ऊर्ध्वं प्राणमुन्नयत्यपानं प्रत्यगस्यति | मध्ये वामनमासीनं विश्वे देवा उपासते ||
ro: ūrdhvaṁ · prāṇam · unnayati · apānaṁ · pratyag · asyati | madhye · vāmanam · āsīnaṁ · viśve · devāḥ · upāsate ||
hi: वह (आत्मा) प्राण को ऊपर ले जाता है और अपान को नीचे फेंकता है। मध्य में (हृदय में) बैठे हुए उस वामन (लघु-आकार, पूजनीय) को सभी देवता उपासना करते हैं।
en: He leads the prāṇa upward and casts the apāna downward. All the gods worship that adorable one (vāmana), who sits in the centre (of the body).

ws.e: upward — the direction of prāṇa (inhalation, ascending vital breath)

ws.h: प्राण को ऊपर ले जाता है
ws.e: leads the prāṇa upward — the Self governs the ascending breath
casts the apāna downward/inward — the Self governs the descending breath; pratyak (inward) + √as (to throw)
the adorable one / the dwarf — vāmana from √vam (to be worthy of worship) or 'small in form'; the Self is 'thumb-sized' (aṅguṣṭha-mātra) yet infinite
all the gods — the cosmic deities and also the sense-faculties (indriyas), which serve the Self
worship — upa + √ās (to sit near, to attend upon); the gods/senses attend upon the Self as servants attend a king

gr: ūrdhvaṁ prāṇam unnayati, apānaṁ pratyag asyati — the Self is the governor of the two primary vital breaths: prāṇa (ascending) and apāna (descending). This shows the Self as the controller of life-functions, not a passive witness. vāmanam — 'the adorable one' or 'the dwarf': connects to the Vedic Vāmana (Viṣṇu's dwarf-avatāra who fills three worlds in three steps) and to the 'thumb-sized Self' (aṅguṣṭha-mātra puruṣa) described later in this Valli. viśve devāḥ upāsate — 'all gods worship': the indriyas (sense-faculties) are the 'gods' who serve the central Self.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_2.1.3 — The verse presents the Self as the controller of prāṇa and apāna — the two fundamental directions of vital breath. This connects to prāṇāyāma practices in yoga. The 'vāmana' sitting in the centre foreshadows the 'thumb-sized puruṣa' (aṅguṣṭha-mātra) described in mantras 12-13.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि प्राण और अपान — ये आत्मा के अधीन हैं, आत्मा प्राणों के अधीन नहीं। जैसे राजा सेवकों को आज्ञा देता है, वैसे ही आत्मा प्राणों को संचालित करता है। 'वामन' — आत्मा सूक्ष्म (अंगुष्ठ-मात्र) है पर सर्वव्यापक।
advaita.en: Shankara says prāṇa and apāna are under the Self's command — the Self is not under the prāṇas. Just as a king commands servants, the Self directs the vital breaths. 'Vāmana' — the Self is subtle (thumb-sized) yet all-pervading.
advaita.ins: You breathe, but you do not will each breath — Something breathes through you. That Something is the Self, quietly governing life from the centre.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि भगवान् ही प्राण-अपान के नियन्ता हैं — यह उनकी अन्तर्यामित्व (inner controllership) का प्रमाण है। 'विश्वे देवाः उपासते' — सभी देवता भगवान् की सेवा करते हैं; भगवान् किसी की सेवा नहीं करते।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the Lord is the controller of prāṇa and apāna — this is proof of His inner controllership. 'Viśve devāḥ upāsate' — all the gods serve the Lord; the Lord serves none.
vishisht.ins: Even the gods — Indra, Agni, Vāyu — are servants of the supreme Lord who sits in the heart. What then of the individual ego, which imagines itself to be the master?

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द 'प्राण' और 'अपान' में चेतना की दो गतियाँ देखते हैं — एक ऊर्ध्वमुखी (ascending, evolution) और दूसरी अधोमुखी (descending, involution)। 'वामन' — वह छोटा-सा दिव्य प्रकाश जो हृदय-गुहा में रहता है, psychic being है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo sees in prāṇa and apāna two movements of consciousness — one ascending (evolution) and one descending (involution). The 'vāmana' — that small divine light dwelling in the heart-cave — is the psychic being.
aurobindo.ins: At the centre of all the forces moving up and down in you sits a still point of divine light — the psychic being, the true soul. The gods within you (your higher faculties) instinctively turn toward it.

dp.q: 🔍 What are prāṇa and apāna, and why does the Self govern them?
dp.a: In Vedic physiology, prāṇa and apāna are the two primary directions of vital energy. Prāṇa moves upward (ūrdhva) — governing inhalation, speech, and the ascending functions of life. Apāna moves downward (pratyak/adhah) — governing exhalation, excretion, and the descending functions. Together they create the basic rhythm of life: intake and output, assimilation and release. The verse says the Self governs both — 'unnayati' (leads up) and 'asyati' (casts down). This is significant because it means the Self is not a passive observer but the active controller of the life-process. Without the Self's presence, the prāṇas would have no organising principle — the body would be dead matter. This understanding is the basis of prāṇāyāma in yoga: by consciously regulating the breath, the yogin aligns with the Self's governing activity and gains mastery over the vital forces.

dp.q: 🔍 Who is the 'vāmana' in the centre?
dp.a: The word vāmana has two related meanings: (1) From √vam — 'to be worthy of worship' — it means 'the adorable one.' (2) As a common noun it means 'dwarf' — something small in form. Both meanings converge in the image of the Self as infinitely worthy yet infinitely subtle — small enough to dwell in the heart, yet worshipped by all the gods. This connects to the famous Vāmana avatāra of Viṣṇu, who appeared as a dwarf-boy and then expanded to fill three worlds in three steps — the message being that what appears small contains the infinite. Later in this Valli (mantras 12-13), the Self is described as aṅguṣṭha-mātra puruṣa — the 'thumb-sized person' in the heart. This is the same 'vāmana' — a concentrated point of infinite consciousness. The 'all the gods worship' (viśve devāḥ upāsate) means the indriyas (senses and faculties) function only because they attend upon this central Self.

sk: अस्य विस्रंसमानस्य शरीरस्थस्य देहिनः | देहाद्विमुच्यमानस्य किमत्र परिशिष्यते | एतद्वै तत् ||
ro: asya · visraṁsamānasya · śarīra-sthasya · dehinaḥ | dehāt · vimucyamānasya · kim · atra · pariśiṣyate | etat · vai · tat ||
hi: जब यह शरीर में स्थित देही (आत्मा) — जब यह शरीर विघटित होता है, जब देह से मुक्त होता है — तब यहाँ (इस शरीर में) क्या शेष रहता है? यही वह (ब्रह्म) है।
en: When this embodied Self, dwelling in the body — when the body falls apart and is released from the body — what remains here? This, verily, is That.

ws.e: of that which is falling apart — present participle of vi + √sraṁs (to slip, to disintegrate); the body disintegrating at death
dwelling in the body — śarīra (body) + stha (standing/dwelling); the Self's temporary residence
the embodied one — dehin: one who has a body (deha); the Self as body-bearer
being released from — passive present participle of vi + √muc; the Self departing from the body
what remains here? — pariśiṣyate: 'is left over' from pari + √śiṣ (to leave, to remain); a rhetorical question
this verily is That — the recurring refrain affirming that this teaching points to the ultimate reality

gr: visraṁsamānasya — present middle participle: 'of that which is falling apart'; the body is described in the very process of disintegrating. dehinaḥ — genitive singular: 'of the embodied one'; the Self is called 'dehin' (body-bearer) to show that it carries the body, the body does not carry it. kim atra pariśiṣyate — rhetorical question: 'what remains here?'. The answer is: nothing that matters remains in the body — what matters (the Self) departs. The body is the residue, not the essence.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_2.1.4 — This verse asks the central question of the entire Upanishad from a different angle: not 'does the Self exist after death?' (Nachiketa's original question in 1.1.20) but 'what remains when the Self departs?'. The answer is implicit: the Self takes everything of value when it leaves. The body without the Self is meaningless — like a city without its king. Compare Bhagavad Gītā 2.13: 'dehino'smin yathā dehe.'

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि यह प्रश्न — 'क्या शेष रहता है?' — का उत्तर है: कुछ नहीं (जो मूल्यवान हो)। शरीर जड़ (inert) है; आत्मा के बिना यह मिट्टी मात्र है। जो शेष है वह आत्मा ही है — वह कभी नहीं मरती।
advaita.en: Shankara answers the question 'what remains?' with: nothing of value. The body is inert; without the Self it is mere clay. What truly remains is the Self itself — which never dies.
advaita.ins: The question is not 'what survives death?' but 'what is it that you mistakenly believe dies?'. The Self was never born and never dies — it is the body that falls away, like a worn-out garment.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि देही (आत्मा) देह को छोड़कर भगवान् के साथ रहता है — शरीर में कुछ भी चैतन्य शेष नहीं रहता। आत्मा अजर-अमर है और भगवान् के परम धाम को प्राप्त होती है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the dehin (Self) leaves the body and remains with the Lord — nothing conscious stays behind in the body. The soul is ageless and immortal, and attains the supreme abode of the Lord.
vishisht.ins: Death does not destroy the Self — it merely removes the outermost covering. The soul, accompanied by the Lord, moves on to its next station.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं कि 'किम् अत्र परिशिष्यते?' — यह प्रश्न शरीर के साथ तादात्म्य (identification) को तोड़ने के लिए है। जो शेष रहता है वह भौतिक अवशेष (residue) है — चेतना (consciousness) तो जा चुकी।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'what remains here?' — this question is meant to break identification with the body. What remains is physical residue — the consciousness has already departed.
aurobindo.ins: Look at a dead body and ask: where did the person go? Everything that made them 'them' — consciousness, personality, awareness — has departed. The body was always the instrument, never the musician.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is the Self called 'dehin' (body-bearer)?
dp.a: The term dehin (from deha, 'body') literally means 'the one who has a body' — the body-bearer. This seemingly simple term carries profound philosophical weight. It implies that the Self possesses the body, not the other way around. The body does not 'have a soul' — the soul has a body. This reversal of common perception is the core teaching. The Bhagavad Gītā (2.13) uses the same term: 'dehino'smin yathā dehe kaumāraṁ yauvanaṁ jarā' — 'Just as the embodied one (dehin) passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body, so too does it pass into another body.' The implication is that the Self wears bodies like garments (Gītā 2.22: vāsāṁsi jīrṇāni). The term 'dehin' always signals this teaching: you are not a body with a soul — you are a soul with a body.

dp.q: 🔍 What is the implied answer to 'what remains here'?
dp.a: The question 'kim atra pariśiṣyate?' (what remains here?) is rhetorical — the expected answer is: nothing of essence. When the Self departs, what remains is mere matter — the five elements returning to their source. The body without the Self has no consciousness, no awareness, no personhood. This is why the verse concludes with 'etat vai tat' (this verily is That) — the 'This' that is 'That' (Brahman) is the Self that departs, NOT the body that remains. The Upanishad is making a radical claim: everything you value about a person — their awareness, their love, their intelligence, their identity — is the Self, and it departs completely. The body, which we tend to treat as 'the person', is the leftover, the husk. This understanding is meant to shift the disciple's centre of identity from body to Self.

sk: न प्राणेन नापानेन मर्त्यो जीवति कश्चन | इतरेण तु जीवन्ति यस्मिन्नेतावुपाश्रितौ ||
ro: na · prāṇena · na · apānena · martyaḥ · jīvati · kaścana | itareṇa · tu · jīvanti · yasmin · etau · upāśritau ||
hi: कोई भी मनुष्य न प्राण से जीता है और न अपान से। वे तो किसी अन्य (आत्मा) के आश्रय से जीते हैं — जिसमें ये दोनों (प्राण और अपान) आश्रित हैं।
en: No mortal lives by the prāṇa (inbreath) or by the apāna (outbreath). They live by something else (the Self), in which these two (breaths) have their support.

ws.s: न प्राणेन न अपानेन (na prāṇena na apānena)
ws.h: न प्राण से, न अपान से
ws.e: not by prāṇa, not by apāna — the two main breaths are not the ultimate cause of life
a mortal — one subject to death; from √mṛ (to die)
by another — itara (other/different); the Self, which is distinct from the prāṇas
having their support in — dual nominative: both prāṇa and apāna 'rest upon' the Self; upa + ā + √śri (to lean upon)

gr: na prāṇena na apānena — emphatic double negation: neither the inbreath nor the outbreath is the cause of life. itareṇa tu — 'but by another': this 'other' is left unnamed, forcing the listener to inquire — what is it? The answer is the Self (ātman). yasmin etau upāśritau — 'in which these two are supported': the prāṇas depend on the Self, not the Self on the prāṇas. The Self is the foundation of all life-functions.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_2.1.5 — This verse challenges the Prāṇa-vāda (the doctrine that prāṇa is the ultimate reality), which appears in the Prashna Upanishad and Chāndogya. Here the Katha asserts that prāṇa is itself dependent on something deeper — the Self. This establishes a hierarchy: body < prāṇa < Self.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि प्राण जीवन का साधन (instrument) है, कारण (cause) नहीं। प्राण आत्मा पर आश्रित है; आत्मा प्राण पर नहीं। जैसे दीपक प्रकाश का साधन है पर प्रकाश-स्रोत (अग्नि) नहीं — वैसे ही प्राण जीवन का वाहक है, स्रोत नहीं।
advaita.en: Shankara says prāṇa is the instrument of life, not its cause. Prāṇa depends on the Self; the Self does not depend on prāṇa. Just as a lamp is the vehicle of light but not the source (which is fire) — so prāṇa is the carrier of life, not its source.
advaita.ins: Breath is the symptom of life, not its cause. When the Self withdraws, the breath stops — not the other way around.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि प्राण और अपान भगवान् के नियन्त्रण में कार्य करते हैं। 'इतरेण' — वह 'अन्य' भगवान् (परमात्मा) है, जो सबका आधार है। प्राण स्वतन्त्र नहीं; वह भी भगवान् पर निर्भर है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says prāṇa and apāna function under the Lord's control. 'Itareṇa' — that 'other' is the Lord (Paramātman), the support of all. Prāṇa is not independent; it too depends on the Lord.
vishisht.ins: We think we live because we breathe. In truth, we breathe because the Lord wills it. Remove His will, and the breath cannot sustain itself for a single moment.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं कि प्राण एक शक्ति (force) है, चेतना (consciousness) नहीं। शक्ति चेतना पर आश्रित है, चेतना शक्ति पर नहीं। 'इतरेण' — वह चेतना ही आत्मा है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says prāṇa is a force, not consciousness. Force depends on consciousness, not consciousness on force. 'Itareṇa' — that consciousness is the Self.
aurobindo.ins: Life-force is not life itself — it is consciousness expressing itself through force. Take away consciousness and force has no direction, no purpose, no intelligence.

dp.q: 🔍 If breath doesn't sustain life, what does?
dp.a: This verse makes a startling claim: breath (prāṇa and apāna) is not the cause of life. Modern biology equates life with biological functions — metabolism, respiration, cellular activity. But the Upanishad is pointing to something more fundamental. Consider: why does the breath stop at death? No physical disease need be present — sometimes the body is perfectly intact, yet the person dies. The Upanishad's answer is that consciousness (ātman) is the foundation of life, and the prāṇas (vital breaths) are merely the instruments through which consciousness operates the body. They are like the electricity that runs through a machine — real and necessary, but themselves dependent on a source. When the source (the Self) withdraws, the instruments (the prāṇas) collapse. This establishes a clear hierarchy: body < prāṇa < Self. The body depends on prāṇa; prāṇa depends on the Self; the Self depends on nothing.

dp.q: 🔍 How does this verse challenge the Prāṇa-vāda?
dp.a: Several Upanishads — notably the Prashna Upanishad (Question 2) and Chāndogya (1.2, 5.1) — contain passages that seem to elevate prāṇa to the status of the ultimate principle. In the Chāndogya's famous 'contest of faculties,' prāṇa is declared the supreme faculty because when it begins to depart, all other faculties (speech, sight, hearing, mind) are dragged along with it. This led to the Prāṇa-vāda — the view that prāṇa (vital force) is the highest reality. The Katha Upanishad here corrects this view: prāṇa is indeed supreme among the bodily faculties, but it is not the ultimate reality. There is something itara (other) — the Self — in which even prāṇa and apāna 'have their support' (upāśritau). This 'other' is consciousness itself — not a force but the ground of all forces. The Katha thus establishes the Self, not prāṇa, as the final substratum.

sk: हन्त त इदं प्रवक्ष्यामि गुह्यं ब्रह्म सनातनम् | यथा च मरणं प्राप्य आत्मा भवति गौतम ||
ro: hanta · te · idaṁ · pravakṣyāmi · guhyaṁ · brahma · sanātanam | yathā · ca · maraṇaṁ · prāpya · ātmā · bhavati · gautama ||
hi: हे गौतम (नचिकेता)! सुनो, मैं तुम्हें वह गुह्य (रहस्यमय) सनातन ब्रह्म बताऊँगा — और यह भी कि मृत्यु को प्राप्त होकर आत्मा क्या होता है।
en: Listen! I shall tell you, O Gautama (Nachiketa), this secret, the eternal Brahman — and also what happens to the Self after death.

ws.e: listen! / come! — an exclamatory particle calling attention; marks an important revelation
I shall declare — future tense of pra + √vac (to speak); Yama's promise to reveal
secret, hidden — from √guh (to hide); this teaching is concealed from ordinary perception
eternal, ancient — sanātana: existing from beginningless time; a key attribute of Brahman
having reached death — maraṇa (death) + prāpya (absolutive: having attained); what happens at the moment of death
O Gautama — Nachiketa's gotra (clan) name; he is of the Gautama lineage

gr: hanta — an emphatic particle: 'Come now! Listen!' — signalling that a major revelation follows. guhyaṁ brahma sanātanam — 'the secret eternal Brahman': two attributes of Brahman — it is guhya (hidden, esoteric) and sanātana (eternal, without beginning or end). yathā ca maraṇaṁ prāpya ātmā bhavati — 'and how the Self becomes after reaching death': this directly answers Nachiketa's original question from Valli 1 (1.1.20): 'What happens to a person after death?'.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_2.1.6 — This verse marks a transition: Yama is about to reveal the destinations of the Self after death (mantras 7-8), which explain the mechanics of rebirth. The address 'Gautama' (Nachiketa's gotra name) adds a personal touch — Yama is speaking directly to his disciple. This verse connects back to the original question that opened the entire Upanishad.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'गुह्य' — ब्रह्म इसलिए गुह्य है क्योंकि यह इन्द्रियों से परे है; 'सनातन' — क्योंकि यह कालातीत है। मृत्यु के बाद आत्मा 'क्या होता है' — यह प्रश्न अविद्या से उत्पन्न है, क्योंकि वास्तव में आत्मा कुछ 'होता' नहीं — वह सदा वही रहता है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'guhya' — Brahman is secret because it is beyond the senses; 'sanātana' — because it is beyond time. The question 'what becomes of the Self after death?' arises from avidyā, because in truth the Self does not 'become' anything — it remains always the same.
advaita.ins: The Self does not go anywhere at death — it was never born, so it cannot die. What 'goes' is the subtle body (liṅga-śarīra) carrying impressions. The Self remains what it always was.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि भगवान् 'गुह्य' (रहस्य) इसलिए हैं क्योंकि केवल भक्ति से ही जाने जा सकते हैं, तर्क मात्र से नहीं। मृत्यु के बाद आत्मा कर्मानुसार विभिन्न गतियों को प्राप्त होता है — यही यम अब बताने वाला है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the Lord is 'guhya' (secret) because He can be known only through devotion, not through reasoning alone. After death, the soul attains various destinations according to karma — this is what Yama is about to reveal.
vishisht.ins: The mystery of death is not a philosophical puzzle to be solved by logic — it is a sacred truth revealed by grace to the devoted seeker.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं कि 'गुह्य' का अर्थ है — यह ज्ञान बौद्धिक विश्लेषण से नहीं, आन्तरिक अनुभव से प्राप्त होता है। मृत्यु के बाद आत्मा की गति — यह चेतना की अवस्था पर निर्भर करती है, शरीर की स्थिति पर नहीं।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'guhya' means this knowledge comes from inner experience, not intellectual analysis. The Self's journey after death depends on the state of consciousness, not the condition of the body.
aurobindo.ins: Death is a transition of consciousness, not an end. Where you go depends on where your consciousness stands — its level, its attachments, its realisation.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is Nachiketa addressed as 'Gautama'?
dp.a: Nachiketa is addressed by his gotra (clan) name — Gautama. His father is Vājaśravasa (also called Uddālaka Āruṇi in some recensions), who belongs to the Gautama lineage. The use of the gotra name rather than the personal name is significant: it is a formal mode of address in teacher-student dialogue, acknowledging the student's lineage and thus his eligibility (adhikāra) to receive the teaching. By calling him 'Gautama,' Yama is essentially saying: 'You come from a noble lineage of seekers — you are worthy of this secret teaching.' This is also a literary marker signalling the transition from general philosophical discussion to a specific esoteric revelation — Yama is about to disclose what happens at death, the very question Nachiketa asked in Valli 1.

dp.q: 🔍 What makes Brahman both 'guhya' and 'sanātana'?
dp.a: Guhya (secret/hidden) and sanātana (eternal) describe Brahman's two fundamental characteristics. Guhya — Brahman is hidden not because someone deliberately conceals it, but because it is beyond the reach of the senses and ordinary mind. The eyes see forms, the ears hear sounds — but Brahman is formless and soundless. It is 'hidden' the way space is hidden — it is everywhere, but you cannot point to it or grasp it. The Kena Upanishad (1.3) says: 'na tatra cakṣur gacchati, na vāg gacchati, no manaḥ' — 'The eye does not go there, nor speech, nor the mind.' Sanātana — Brahman is eternal not in the sense of lasting a very long time, but in the sense of being outside time altogether. It was not created and will not be destroyed because it never entered the stream of time. Past, present, and future are categories of the mind; Brahman is the ground on which the mind (and therefore time) operates. Together, these two qualities explain why Brahman must be revealed (pravakṣyāmi — 'I shall declare') rather than discovered — what is hidden and eternal cannot be found by ordinary search; it must be shown by one who knows.

sk: योनिमन्ये प्रपद्यन्ते शरीरत्वाय देहिनः | स्थाणुमन्येऽनुसंयन्ति यथाकर्म यथाश्रुतम् ||
ro: yonim · anye · prapadyante · śarīratvāya · dehinaḥ | sthāṇum · anye · anusaṁyanti · yathā-karma · yathā-śrutam ||
hi: कुछ देही (आत्माएँ) पुनः शरीर प्राप्त करने के लिए योनि (गर्भ) में प्रवेश करते हैं; अन्य स्थावर (वृक्ष आदि) में जाते हैं — अपने-अपने कर्म और ज्ञान के अनुसार।
en: Some embodied souls enter a womb to gain a body again; others pass into stationary forms (like trees and plants) — according to their karma and according to their knowledge.

ws.e: womb — yoni: the point of origin; here specifically the womb, indicating rebirth as a moving (jaṅgama) being
they enter — pra + √pad (to go forth into); they take birth
for the purpose of embodiment — dative of purpose: 'in order to have a body'
stationary forms — sthāṇu: immovable beings like trees, plants, rocks; a lower form of birth
they pass into — anu + sam + √yā (to go along with); they attain that form
according to their karma — yathā (as per) + karma (action); the quality of past actions determines the next birth
according to their knowledge — yathā (as per) + śruta (what was heard/learned); spiritual understanding also determines destiny

gr: anye ... anye — 'some ... others': a contrast between two types of post-death destinations. yonim prapadyante — entering a womb: rebirth as a sentient, mobile being (human, animal, etc.). sthāṇum anusaṁyanti — passing into stationary forms: rebirth as a tree, plant, or mineral — considered a lower birth due to restricted consciousness. yathā-karma yathā-śrutam — two factors determine the destination: (1) karma — accumulated actions; (2) śruta — knowledge acquired. Both matter — action without knowledge and knowledge without action both have consequences.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_2.1.7 — This verse answers the question posed in mantra 6: what happens to the Self after death. The doctrine of karma and rebirth is stated concisely. The dual criterion — yathā-karma AND yathā-śrutam — shows that the Upanishad values both ethical action and spiritual knowledge. Compare Brihadaranyaka 4.4.5: 'sa yathā-karmī yathā-vidyī tathā bhavati' — 'as is his action, as is his knowledge, so does he become.'

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि पुनर्जन्म अविद्या का फल है — ज्ञानी को पुनर्जन्म नहीं होता। 'यथा-कर्म' — कर्म गति (destination) निर्धारित करता है; 'यथा-श्रुतम्' — ज्ञान मुक्ति देता है। जो दोनों से रहित है वह स्थावर योनि में जाता है।
advaita.en: Shankara says rebirth is the result of avidyā — the wise one is not reborn. 'Yathā-karma' — karma determines the destination; 'yathā-śrutam' — knowledge grants liberation. One lacking both goes to stationary forms.
advaita.ins: Rebirth is not punishment — it is the natural consequence of unfinished business. The soul is drawn to the form that best matches its accumulated tendencies and understanding.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि जीवात्मा कर्मानुसार विभिन्न शरीर प्राप्त करता है — यह भगवान् की न्यायपूर्ण व्यवस्था है। भक्ति और सत्कर्म से उत्तम गति; अज्ञान और दुष्कर्म से अधम गति।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the jīvātman obtains different bodies according to karma — this is the Lord's just arrangement. Devotion and good deeds lead to higher birth; ignorance and evil deeds lead to lower birth.
vishisht.ins: The law of karma is not blind fate — it is the Lord's justice operating through natural law. Every action is a seed; every birth is a harvest.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द पुनर्जन्म को चेतना के विकास (evolution of consciousness) के दृष्टिकोण से देखते हैं — आत्मा विभिन्न शरीरों में अनुभव एकत्र करती है, प्रत्येक जन्म एक नया अध्याय है। 'स्थाणु' — चेतना का सुप्त (dormant) रूप; 'योनि' — चेतना का सक्रिय (active) रूप।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo views rebirth from the perspective of the evolution of consciousness — the soul gathers experience through different bodies; each birth is a new chapter. 'Sthāṇu' — a dormant form of consciousness; 'yoni' — an active form of consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: Rebirth is not a cycle of punishment and reward — it is the soul's curriculum. Each life is a lesson, each body a classroom. The soul chooses (or is drawn to) what it needs to learn next.

dp.q: 🔍 What determines the destination of the soul after death?
dp.a: The verse gives two factors that determine where the soul goes: yathā-karma (according to action) and yathā-śrutam (according to knowledge). These are not alternatives but co-determinants. Karma includes all accumulated actions — physical, verbal, and mental. Good karma leads to higher births (human or divine); bad karma leads to lower births (animal or stationary). But karma alone does not explain everything — the Brihadaranyaka (4.4.5) adds 'yathā-vidyī' (according to knowledge), showing that understanding also shapes destiny. Śruta (literally 'what was heard') refers to spiritual knowledge — the Vedas, the Upanishads, the teachings of a guru. Knowledge can override karma: even with some residual karma, a person with deep spiritual knowledge can attain liberation. Conversely, good karma without knowledge leads to heavenly rewards that eventually expire, sending the soul back to rebirth. The ideal combination is both: righteous action AND spiritual knowledge.

dp.q: 🔍 What are 'stationary forms' (sthāṇu) and why are they significant?
dp.a: The word sthāṇu (from √sthā, 'to stand') refers to immovable living beings — trees, plants, and by extension minerals and rocks. In the Indian classification of life, beings are divided into jaṅgama (mobile: humans, animals, birds) and sthāvara (stationary: trees, plants). Birth as a sthāvara is considered a lower birth because consciousness is highly restricted — a tree cannot move, speak, think, or seek liberation. It is a form of near-complete dormancy of consciousness. The Manu Smṛti (1.46-50) describes a hierarchy: plants < insects < animals < humans < celestials. Going 'into a sthāṇu' means the soul's consciousness has contracted to a minimal level due to the weight of tamasic karma and absence of knowledge. This is not eternal damnation — even from the lowest form, the soul eventually works its way back up through the cycle. But the message is sobering: without knowledge and right action, consciousness can regress, not just stagnate.

sk: य एष सुप्तेषु जागर्ति कामं कामं पुरुषो निर्मिमाणः | तदेव शुक्रं तद्ब्रह्म तदेवामृतमुच्यते | तस्मिंल्लोकाः श्रिताः सर्वे तदु नात्येति कश्चन | एतद्वै तत् ||
ro: yaḥ · eṣaḥ · supteṣu · jāgarti · kāmaṁ · kāmaṁ · puruṣaḥ · nirmimāṇaḥ | tat · eva · śukraṁ · tat · brahma · tat · eva · amṛtam · ucyate | tasmin · lokāḥ · śritāḥ · sarve · tat · u · na · atyeti · kaścana | etat · vai · tat ||
hi: जो यह पुरुष (आत्मा) सोने वालों में (सभी प्राणियों के सोने पर भी) जागता रहता है, और इच्छा-इच्छा (विविध कामनाओं) को निर्मित (shape) करता है — वही शुक्र (शुद्ध प्रकाश) है, वही ब्रह्म है, वही अमृत कहा जाता है। सभी लोक (worlds) उसी में आश्रित हैं; उसे कोई भी अतिक्रमण (transcend) नहीं कर सकता। यही वह (ब्रह्म) है।
en: This Puruṣa who wakes while all beings sleep, shaping desire after desire — He alone is the Pure (Light), He is Brahman, He alone is called the Immortal. All worlds rest in Him; none can go beyond Him. This, verily, is That.

ws.e: among those who sleep — locative plural; all beings are 'asleep' in ignorance; also the dream-state where the Self alone remains awake
wakes / keeps vigil — the Self is the eternal witness, never unconscious
desire after desire — the repetition indicates multiplicity; the Self projects the dream-world of desires
shaping / fashioning — present participle of nir + √mā (to measure out, to create); the Self creates the dream-experience
the pure / the radiant — śukra: bright, white, pure; the Self's essential nature is luminous purity
the immortal — a (not) + mṛta (dead); deathlessness, the nectar of immortality
none goes beyond — na atyeti: does not surpass; Brahman is the unsurpassable limit of reality

gr: supteṣu jāgarti — 'wakes among the sleeping': the Self is the one constant awareness that persists through waking, dream, and deep sleep. When the body sleeps, the Self is awake. kāmaṁ kāmaṁ nirmimāṇaḥ — 'fashioning desire after desire': in the dream-state, the Self projects an entire world of experiences out of stored impressions (vāsanās). śukraṁ ... brahma ... amṛtam — three names for the same reality: the Pure, Brahman, the Immortal. tasmin lokāḥ śritāḥ sarve — 'all worlds rest in Him': Brahman is not within the worlds — the worlds are within Brahman.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_2.1.8 — This is one of the most important verses in the Katha, identifying the Self with the dreamer who creates the dream-world. The verse appears identically in Rig Veda 10.? (adapted). The three-fold identification (śukra + brahma + amṛta) and the phrase 'tadu nātyeti kaścana' (none surpasses Him) establish Brahman as the absolute ceiling of reality. Compare Taittirīya 2.1: 'satyaṁ jñānam anantaṁ brahma.'

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'सुप्तेषु जागर्ति' — आत्मा चेतना का शाश्वत साक्षी है; वह कभी सोता नहीं। स्वप्न में जो विविध दृश्य दिखते हैं, वे आत्मा की माया-शक्ति से प्रकट होते हैं। जाग्रत, स्वप्न, सुषुप्ति — तीनों अवस्थाओं में आत्मा एक ही रहता है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'supteṣu jāgarti' — the Self is the eternal witness of consciousness; it never sleeps. The various scenes in dreams are projected by the Self's māyā-power. In waking, dream, and deep sleep — the Self remains one and the same.
advaita.ins: You sleep, but awareness does not. Who notices the transition from waking to dreaming? Who registers the blankness of deep sleep? That unchanging witness is the Self.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि भगवान् सदा जागते हैं — सभी प्राणियों की सुषुप्ति (deep sleep) में भी वे सचेत हैं और सबकी रक्षा करते हैं। 'कामं कामं निर्मिमाणः' — भगवान् ही कर्मफलानुसार प्रत्येक जीव की भोग-सृष्टि (experiential world) की रचना करते हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the Lord is ever-awake — even in the deep sleep of all beings, He is conscious and protects all. 'Kāmaṁ kāmaṁ nirmimāṇaḥ' — the Lord fashions each being's experiential world according to their karma.
vishisht.ins: When you sleep, the Lord watches over you. When the universe dissolves, the Lord remains awake. His vigilance is the guarantee of cosmic order.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं कि 'सुप्तेषु जागर्ति' — यह सुप्राचेतन (supramental) चेतना का वर्णन है जो सामान्य मन की निद्रा में भी सक्रिय रहती है। स्वप्न-निर्माण चेतना की सृजनात्मक शक्ति (creative power) का प्रमाण है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'supteṣu jāgarti' describes the supramental consciousness that remains active even in the sleep of the ordinary mind. Dream-creation is evidence of consciousness's creative power.
aurobindo.ins: The fact that you create entire worlds in your dreams — with landscapes, people, emotions, events — proves that consciousness is fundamentally creative. In waking life, the same power creates the experience of reality.

dp.q: 🔍 How does the Self 'wake while others sleep'?
dp.a: The phrase 'supteṣu jāgarti' operates on two levels. Literally: when the body and mind fall asleep, the Self remains awake — it is the awareness that knows sleep is happening. You wake up and say 'I slept well' — who registered that quality of sleep? Not the sleeping mind, which was inactive. It was the Self, the constant witness that never sleeps. Metaphorically: all beings are 'asleep' in the sense of being ignorant of their true nature. They go through life without recognising the Self within. But the Self is fully 'awake' — fully conscious — even while the beings it inhabits are unaware of it. The dream-state is the most vivid illustration: when the external senses shut down and the mind turns inward, the Self creates an entire experiential world out of its own substance — 'kāmaṁ kāmaṁ nirmimāṇaḥ' (fashioning desire after desire). This creative activity in dreams is evidence that consciousness is prior to the external world, not derived from it.

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'none can go beyond Him' (na atyeti kaścana) mean?
dp.a: The phrase 'tad u nātyeti kaścana' — 'none whatsoever goes beyond That' — establishes Brahman as the absolute limit of reality. There is nothing higher, nothing beyond, nothing outside. This is not a claim of magnitude ('He is very big') but of totality — Brahman is the ground of all existence, and you cannot go beyond the ground on which you stand. The statement echoes the Katha's own teaching from 1.3.11: the hierarchy of being ascends from senses → mind → buddhi → mahān ātmā → avyakta → puruṣa, and then: 'puruṣān na paraṁ kiñcit — sā kāṣṭhā sā parā gatiḥ' — 'There is nothing beyond the Puruṣa — that is the limit, that is the highest goal.' 'All worlds rest in Him' (tasmin lokāḥ śritāḥ sarve) completes the picture: Brahman is not in the universe — the universe is in Brahman. To 'go beyond' Brahman would mean stepping outside reality itself — which is logically impossible.

sk: अग्निर्यथैको भुवनं प्रविष्टो रूपं रूपं प्रतिरूपो बभूव | एकस्तथा सर्वभूतान्तरात्मा रूपं रूपं प्रतिरूपो बहिश्च ||
ro: agniḥ · yathā · ekaḥ · bhuvanaṁ · praviṣṭaḥ · rūpaṁ · rūpaṁ · pratirūpaḥ · babhūva | ekaḥ · tathā · sarva-bhūta-antarātmā · rūpaṁ · rūpaṁ · pratirūpaḥ · bahiḥ · ca ||
hi: जैसे एक ही अग्नि संसार में प्रविष्ट होकर प्रत्येक रूप के अनुसार (प्रतिरूप) बन जाती है — वैसे ही एक ही सर्वभूतान्तरात्मा (सभी प्राणियों का भीतरी आत्मा) प्रत्येक रूप के अनुसार बनता है और (सबके) बाहर भी है।
en: Just as the one fire, having entered the world, takes on the form of each shape (it burns in) — so the one inner Self of all beings takes the form of each form, and is also beyond (them all).

ws.e: just as the one fire — fire is one universal element, but it takes different shapes in different fuels
having entered the world — the fire enters the world and manifests in different forms
conforming to each form — pratirūpa: counter-form, matching form; fire in wood looks different from fire in oil
the inner Self of all beings — the compound: sarva (all) + bhūta (beings) + antar (inner) + ātmā (Self)
and also outside — bahis (outside); the Self is both immanent and transcendent

gr: agniḥ yathā ekaḥ — the fire-analogy: one fire, many shapes. The fire that burns in a lamp, a forest, and a kitchen is the same fire — but it looks different in each. rūpaṁ rūpaṁ pratirūpaḥ — 'matching form after form': the Self takes on the appearance of each being it inhabits, just as fire takes on the shape of what it burns. sarva-bhūta-antarātmā — a magnificent compound: 'the inner Self of all beings'; this is the Self not as a personal possession but as the universal presence within everything. bahiḥ ca — 'and outside too': the Self is not confined to the interior — it also transcends all forms. This adds the dimension of transcendence to immanence.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_2.1.9 — This verse (and the following four) present a series of analogies for the Self's simultaneous immanence and transcendence. The fire-analogy is the first. Compare Shvetashvatara 6.11: 'eko devaḥ sarva-bhūteṣu gūḍhaḥ' — 'the one God hidden in all beings.' The Bhagavad Gītā (13.16) echoes: 'bahir antaś ca bhūtānām' — 'inside and outside of all beings.'

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि जैसे अग्नि एक होकर भी भिन्न-भिन्न रूपों में दिखती है — वैसे ही ब्रह्म एक होकर भी अनेक शरीरों में भिन्न प्रतीत होता है। भिन्नता आभासिक (apparent) है, एकता वास्तविक है। 'बहिश्च' — ब्रह्म शरीरों में ही नहीं, शरीरों से बाहर भी है।
advaita.en: Shankara says just as fire is one yet appears different in different forms — so Brahman is one yet appears different in different bodies. The difference is apparent; the unity is real. 'Bahiś ca' — Brahman is not only in bodies but also beyond them.
advaita.ins: The fire in a candle and the fire in a forest are the same fire. The Self in an ant and the Self in a saint are the same Self. Seeing diversity is natural; seeing the unity within diversity is wisdom.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि भगवान् एक होकर भी सभी जीवों में अन्तर्यामी रूप से विराजमान हैं — पर वे प्रत्येक शरीर की सीमा में बँधते नहीं, बल्कि सबसे परे भी हैं। अग्नि उपमा यह दर्शाती है कि भगवान् विश्व में व्याप्त हैं पर विश्व द्वारा सीमित नहीं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the Lord, though one, dwells as the inner controller in all beings — yet He is not confined by any body but also exists beyond all. The fire-analogy shows the Lord pervades the world yet is not limited by it.
vishisht.ins: God enters every form yet remains Himself — undiminished, undistorted. A million candle-flames do not exhaust the fire.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं कि अग्नि-उपमा चेतना की अनन्त अनुकूलनशीलता (infinite adaptability) को दर्शाती है — एक ही दिव्य चेतना चींटी में, मनुष्य में, देवता में — प्रत्येक में उसी रूप में प्रकट होती है जो उस पात्र (vessel) की क्षमता है। 'बहिश्च' — और सबसे परे भी।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says the fire-analogy shows consciousness's infinite adaptability — the same divine consciousness manifests in an ant, a human, a god — each according to the vessel's capacity. 'Bahiś ca' — and beyond them all.
aurobindo.ins: Consciousness is not one-size-fits-all — it pours itself into each form perfectly, taking the shape of its container. The ocean in a cup is still the ocean.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is fire chosen as the analogy for the Self?
dp.a: Fire (agni) is perhaps the most apt analogy for the Self because it shares several key properties: (1) One yet many: there is one 'fire-principle' but it manifests differently in a candle, a forest fire, a kitchen stove, and the sun — just as one Self manifests differently in an ant, a human, and a deity. (2) Transforms but is not consumed: fire transforms fuel but remains fire — the Self inhabits bodies but remains unchanged. (3) Hidden until manifested: fire is latent in wood (as friction-fire) and becomes visible when drawn out — the Self is latent in beings and becomes 'visible' through spiritual practice. (4) Luminous: fire is self-luminous (svayaṁ-prakāśa) — it reveals other things without needing to be revealed itself, just as consciousness illuminates experience without needing another consciousness to illumine it. The Vedas consistently use fire (Agni) as the primary symbol of the divine — the very first word of the Rig Veda is 'agnim.'

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'bahiḥ ca' (and outside too) add to the teaching?
dp.a: The phrase 'bahiḥ ca' (and outside too) prevents a common misunderstanding: that the Self is only immanent — only inside things. If the Self were only internal, it would be limited by the forms it inhabits — just as water in a glass is shaped and bounded by the glass. By adding 'bahiḥ ca,' the Upanishad asserts that the Self is also transcendent — it exceeds every form it inhabits. The Self in a human body is not confined to that body; it also exists beyond it, pervading space itself. This is the doctrine of simultaneous immanence and transcendence — the Self is fully present in every being AND fully beyond every being at the same time. The Bhagavad Gītā (9.4-5) expresses this paradox directly: 'mayā tatam idaṁ sarvaṁ jagat avyakta-mūrtinā; mat-sthāni sarva-bhūtāni, na cāhaṁ teṣv avasthitaḥ' — 'I pervade this entire world in My unmanifest form; all beings are in Me, yet I am not in them.' This is the mystery: the infinite can be fully in the finite without being reduced to it.

sk: वायुर्यथैको भुवनं प्रविष्टो रूपं रूपं प्रतिरूपो बभूव | एकस्तथा सर्वभूतान्तरात्मा रूपं रूपं प्रतिरूपो बहिश्च ||
ro: vāyuḥ · yathā · ekaḥ · bhuvanaṁ · praviṣṭaḥ · rūpaṁ · rūpaṁ · pratirūpaḥ · babhūva | ekaḥ · tathā · sarva-bhūta-antarātmā · rūpaṁ · rūpaṁ · pratirūpaḥ · bahiḥ · ca ||
hi: जैसे एक ही वायु संसार में प्रविष्ट होकर प्रत्येक रूप के अनुसार बन जाती है — वैसे ही एक ही सर्वभूतान्तरात्मा (सभी प्राणियों का भीतरी आत्मा) प्रत्येक रूप के अनुसार बनता है और (सबके) बाहर भी है।
en: Just as the one wind (vāyu), having entered the world, takes on the form of each shape — so the one inner Self of all beings takes the form of each form, and is also beyond (them all).

ws.e: wind — vāyu: the universal air/wind; one element that takes different forms (breeze, storm, breath)
having entered the world — the wind enters and pervades the world
conforming to each form — wind in a flute sounds different from wind in a storm, yet it is the same air
the inner Self of all beings — same compound as the previous verse; the one universal Self
and also outside — the Self transcends all forms even while pervading them

gr: vāyuḥ yathā ekaḥ — the wind-analogy: structurally identical to the fire-analogy (mantra 9), but using wind instead of fire. Wind is formless, invisible, and all-pervading — an even more apt image for the Self. rūpaṁ rūpaṁ pratirūpaḥ — wind takes on the 'form' of whatever it passes through: a gentle breeze through trees, a howling gale in a canyon, the breath in human lungs — yet it is the same air. bahiḥ ca — again emphasising transcendence alongside immanence.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_2.1.10 — This verse is structurally identical to mantra 9, substituting vāyu (wind) for agni (fire). The pair agni-vāyu represents two of the three great cosmic forces in Vedic thought (the third being āditya/sun). Wind adds the quality of invisibility — unlike fire, you cannot see wind, only its effects. This makes it an even better analogy for the invisible Self.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि अग्नि-दृष्टान्त के बाद वायु-दृष्टान्त यह दर्शाता है कि आत्मा अदृश्य (invisible) भी है — जैसे वायु दिखती नहीं पर अनुभव होती है, वैसे ही आत्मा दिखता नहीं पर उसके प्रभाव (effects) — चेतना, प्राण, जीवन — ये सब दिखते हैं।
advaita.en: Shankara says after the fire-analogy, the wind-analogy shows the Self is also invisible — just as wind is not seen but felt, the Self is not seen but its effects — consciousness, prāṇa, life — are evident.
advaita.ins: You cannot see the wind — but you can feel it, hear it, see its effects on trees and water. Similarly, you cannot see the Self — but everything you experience is its effect.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि वायु-उपमा भगवान् की सूक्ष्म-व्यापकता (subtle pervasion) दर्शाती है — जैसे वायु हर स्थान में प्रवेश कर जाती है, वैसे ही भगवान् हर आत्मा में व्याप्त हैं, पर उनसे भिन्न और स्वतन्त्र हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the wind-analogy shows the Lord's subtle pervasion — just as wind enters every space, the Lord pervades every soul, yet remains distinct and independent of them.
vishisht.ins: Wind fills every room yet belongs to no room. The Lord enters every soul yet is bound by no soul.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द वायु में चेतना की गतिशील शक्ति (dynamic force) देखते हैं — अग्नि रूपान्तरण (transformation) का प्रतीक है, वायु गति (movement) का। चेतना स्थिर भी है और गतिशील भी — दोनों उपमाएँ मिलकर पूर्ण चित्र देती हैं।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo sees in wind the dynamic force of consciousness — fire symbolises transformation, wind symbolises movement. Consciousness is both still and dynamic — both analogies together give the complete picture.
aurobindo.ins: Fire transforms; wind moves. Consciousness does both — it transforms whatever it touches and it moves through everything without obstruction.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does the Upanishad repeat the same structure with different elements?
dp.a: Mantras 9-12 form a series of analogies with nearly identical structure but different elements — fire (9), wind (10), sun (11), and space (implied). This is a deliberate pedagogical technique: by repeating the same truth through different images, the teacher ensures the student grasps the principle rather than getting attached to any single metaphor. Each element adds a new dimension: Fire (mantra 9) — highlights luminosity and transformation; the Self illuminates and transforms. Wind (mantra 10) — highlights invisibility and pervasion; the Self is unseen yet felt everywhere. The upcoming sun-analogy (mantra 11) will highlight independence from contact. By stacking these analogies, the Upanishad builds a multi-dimensional understanding of the Self that no single metaphor could provide.

dp.q: 🔍 What does wind add that fire does not?
dp.a: Wind (vāyu) complements fire (agni) by adding the quality of formlessness and invisibility. Fire, while luminous, is visible — you can point to a flame, photograph it, measure its heat. Wind is invisible — you know it only through its effects: rustling leaves, moving clouds, the sensation on your skin. This makes wind a superior analogy for the Self in one crucial respect: the Self, like wind, is never directly perceived by the senses. You cannot see it, hear it, touch it, taste it, or smell it (as Katha 1.3.15 stated: 'aśabdam asparśam arūpam'). Yet its effects are everywhere — consciousness, life, intelligence, awareness. The wind-analogy also adds universality of access: wind enters every crack, every space, every crevice — nothing is sealed against it. Similarly, the Self pervades every being without exception, from the largest to the smallest, from the highest to the lowest.

sk: सूर्यो यथा सर्वलोकस्य चक्षुर्न लिप्यते चाक्षुषैर्बाह्यदोषैः | एकस्तथा सर्वभूतान्तरात्मा न लिप्यते लोकदुःखेन बाह्यः ||
ro: sūryaḥ · yathā · sarva-lokasya · cakṣuḥ · na · lipyate · cākṣuṣaiḥ · bāhya-doṣaiḥ | ekaḥ · tathā · sarva-bhūta-antarātmā · na · lipyate · loka-duḥkhena · bāhyaḥ ||
hi: जैसे सूर्य — जो समस्त संसार की आँख है — बाहरी नेत्र-दोषों (जैसे अन्धापन, मोतियाबिन्द) से लिप्त (दूषित) नहीं होता — वैसे ही एक सर्वभूतान्तरात्मा संसार के दुःख से लिप्त नहीं होता — वह (सबसे) बाह्य (बाहर/परे) है।
en: Just as the sun — the eye of the whole world — is not tainted by the external defects of the eyes (that see it) — so the one inner Self of all beings is not tainted by the suffering of the world, for He is beyond (it all).

ws.e: the sun — the universal source of light; analogy for the Self as the illuminator of all experience
the eye of the whole world — the sun makes sight possible; without it, nothing is visible
is not tainted — from √lip (to smear, to stain); the sun is untouched by what it illuminates
by external defects of the eye — cākṣuṣa (pertaining to the eye) + bāhya (external) + doṣa (fault); cataracts, blindness, etc. are defects of the eye, not of the sun
by the suffering of the world — the totality of worldly pain and sorrow
external / beyond — the Self stands outside worldly suffering; it is transcendent

gr: sūryaḥ yathā sarva-lokasya cakṣuḥ — the sun as 'the world's eye' (cakṣuḥ) — a Vedic image. The sun enables all seeing, but the defects of individual eyes do not affect the sun. na lipyate — 'is not smeared/tainted': the Self is untouched by the suffering of the beings it inhabits. cākṣuṣaiḥ bāhya-doṣaiḥ — a blind person's blindness is a defect of their eye, not of the sun — similarly, a being's suffering is a condition of their body/mind, not of the Self. bāhyaḥ — 'external/beyond': the Self transcends worldly suffering, even while pervading the world.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_2.1.11 — This sun-analogy is the most important of the series because it addresses the problem of suffering: if the Self is in all beings, is it tainted by their suffering? The answer is no — just as the sun is untainted by defective eyes. This verse appears nearly identically in the Shvetashvatara Upanishad (6.11) and is echoed in the Bhagavad Gītā (13.33): 'yathā sarva-gataṁ saukṣmyād ākāśaṁ nopalipyate.'

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि यह मन्त्र आत्मा की असंगता (non-attachment) सिद्ध करता है। शरीर में सुख-दुःख होता है, आत्मा में नहीं — जैसे आँख में रोग होता है, सूर्य में नहीं। आत्मा नित्य-शुद्ध, नित्य-मुक्त है।
advaita.en: Shankara says this verse proves the Self's non-attachment (asaṅgatva). Pleasure and pain occur in the body, not in the Self — as disease occurs in the eye, not in the sun. The Self is eternally pure, eternally free.
advaita.ins: If you have a cataract, the world looks blurred — but the sun is perfectly clear. If your body suffers, the suffering is in the body-mind complex — the Self witnesses it untouched.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि भगवान् सभी प्राणियों में हैं पर उनके दुःख से अस्पृष्ट (untouched) हैं — जैसे राजा दरिद्रों के बीच रहे पर दरिद्र नहीं होता। भगवान् की पवित्रता अचल (immutable) है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the Lord is in all beings yet untouched by their suffering — as a king among paupers is not himself a pauper. The Lord's purity is immutable.
vishisht.ins: The Lord enters the suffering world out of compassion but does not suffer Himself — His purity is the guarantee that suffering is not the final reality.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं कि सूर्य-उपमा यह सिद्ध करती है कि दुःख (suffering) आत्मा का गुण नहीं, बल्कि अज्ञानमय चेतना (ignorant consciousness) का गुण है। जैसे नेत्र-रोग सूर्य का नहीं — वैसे ही दुःख आत्मा का नहीं।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says the sun-analogy proves that suffering is not a property of the Self but of ignorant consciousness. As eye-disease is not the sun's fault — so suffering is not the Self's condition.
aurobindo.ins: Suffering is real at the level of mind and body — but it is not the truth of your being. Behind the suffering stands a consciousness as untouched and luminous as the sun behind the clouds.

dp.q: 🔍 How can the Self be 'in' all beings yet untouched by suffering?
dp.a: This is one of the most profound questions in philosophy: if God/the Self is present in every being, does it suffer along with them? The Katha's answer, via the sun-analogy, is a clear no. The logic is precise: a person with cataracts sees the world blurred, but the sun is not blurred — the defect is in the receiving instrument (the eye), not in the source (the sun). Similarly, suffering occurs in the body-mind complex (the receiving instrument), not in the Self (the source of consciousness). The Self illuminates suffering — it is the light by which you know you are suffering — but it is not itself suffering. Think of it this way: a mirror reflects a fire, but the mirror does not burn. The Self reflects all experiences — pleasure, pain, grief, joy — without being affected by any of them. This is what Advaita Vedānta calls sākṣi-caitanya — witness-consciousness: the Self that sees all without being touched by what it sees.

dp.q: 🔍 What is the relationship between this verse and the Bhagavad Gītā?
dp.a: This verse resonates strongly with several Gītā passages. Gītā 13.33 uses a nearly identical analogy: 'yathā sarva-gataṁ saukṣmyād ākāśaṁ nopalipyate, sarvatrāvasthito dehe tathātmā nopalipyate' — 'Just as the all-pervading space, due to its subtlety, is not tainted, so the Self, though dwelling everywhere in the body, is not tainted.' Gītā 5.15: 'nādatte kasyacit pāpaṁ na caiva sukṛtaṁ vibhuḥ' — 'The all-pervading Lord does not take anyone's sin or merit.' Gītā 13.32: 'anāditvān nirguṇatvāt paramātmā'yam avyayaḥ, śarīra-stho'pi kaunteya na karoti na lipyate' — 'Being beginningless and without guṇas, this imperishable supreme Self, though dwelling in the body, neither acts nor is tainted.' The Katha's sun-analogy is the original source that Kṛṣṇa's teaching draws upon. Both texts make the same radical claim: the Self is IN the body but not OF the body — it is present without being implicated.

sk: एको वशी सर्वभूतान्तरात्मा एकं रूपं बहुधा यः करोति | तमात्मस्थं येऽनुपश्यन्ति धीरास्तेषां सुखं शाश्वतं नेतरेषाम् ||
ro: ekaḥ · vaśī · sarva-bhūta-antarātmā · ekaṁ · rūpaṁ · bahudhā · yaḥ · karoti | tam · ātma-sthaṁ · ye · anupaśyanti · dhīrāḥ · teṣāṁ · sukhaṁ · śāśvataṁ · na · itareṣām ||
hi: एक, वशी (सबके नियन्ता), सर्वभूतान्तरात्मा — जो अपने एक रूप को बहुधा (अनेक रूपों में) बनाता है — जो धीर (बुद्धिमान) उसे आत्मस्थ (अपने आत्मा में स्थित) देखते हैं, उनको शाश्वत सुख है — दूसरों को नहीं।
en: The one controller, the inner Self of all beings, who makes His one form manifold — the wise who see Him established in their own Self, to them belongs eternal bliss, and to no others.

ws.e: the one controller — eka (one) + vaśin (having mastery, from √vaś 'to will/control'); the Self rules all from within

ws.s: एकम् रूपम् बहुधा करोति (ekaṁ rūpaṁ bahudhā karoti)
ws.h: एक रूप को अनेक बनाता है
ws.e: makes the one form manifold — the Self multiplies its single nature into countless forms; the creative power of Brahman
established in the Self — ātma (Self) + stha (standing); the Self is found within one's own being
they see / they perceive — anu + √paś (to see); meditative perception, not ordinary seeing
the wise / the steadfast — dhīra: one with stable intelligence; those who can sustain contemplation
eternal bliss — śāśvata (perpetual) + sukha (happiness); not temporary pleasure but permanent fulfilment
not to others — itara (other); those who do not see the Self are excluded from eternal bliss

gr: ekaḥ vaśī — 'the one controller': the Self is not just a passive witness but an active sovereign. ekaṁ rūpaṁ bahudhā yaḥ karoti — 'who makes the one form manifold': the many forms of the world are the Self's own self-multiplication — not the creation of a separate material. ātma-stham — 'established in the Self': the search for the Self does not go outward but inward — the Self is found in one's own being. teṣāṁ sukhaṁ śāśvatam, na itareṣām — a sharp exclusion: eternal bliss belongs ONLY to those who see the Self, and to NO ONE ELSE.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_2.1.12 — This verse combines the ontological teaching (the Self makes one form into many) with the soteriological promise (those who see this gain eternal bliss). The phrase 'teṣāṁ sukhaṁ śāśvataṁ netareṣām' appears also in Shvetashvatara 6.12, nearly identical. The exclusion — 'not to others' — is not cruelty but a statement of natural law: only those who open their eyes can see the sun.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'एकं रूपं बहुधा करोति' — ब्रह्म माया के माध्यम से एक ही सत्ता को अनेक रूपों में प्रकट करता है। जो इस भेद-दर्शन (seeing difference) को पार करके एकत्व देखता है, वही शाश्वत सुख पाता है। 'नेतरेषाम्' — जो भेद में ही रहता है, उसे यह सुख नहीं।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'ekaṁ rūpaṁ bahudhā karoti' — Brahman, through māyā, manifests one being as many forms. One who sees past this apparent diversity to the underlying unity attains eternal bliss. 'Na itareṣām' — one who remains in diversity does not.
advaita.ins: The world looks like many things — but it is one thing wearing many masks. See through the masks, and eternal bliss is yours. Remain deceived by the masks, and the search continues.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि 'एकः वशी' — भगवान् एक हैं और सबके नियन्ता हैं। वे अपनी ही शक्ति से अनेक रूप रचते हैं। जो भक्त उन्हें अपने हृदय में (आत्मस्थम्) देखता है — उसे शाश्वत सुख (मोक्ष) प्राप्त होता है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'ekaḥ vaśī' — the Lord is one and the controller of all. He creates many forms by His own power. The devotee who sees Him in their own heart (ātma-stham) attains eternal bliss (mokṣa).
vishisht.ins: Eternal happiness is not a reward handed out after death — it is the natural state of one who sees God in their own heart, here and now.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं कि 'एकं रूपं बहुधा करोति' — यह एक चेतना की लीला (divine play) है — जो स्वयं को अनेक रूपों में अभिव्यक्त करती है। 'आत्मस्थम्' — इसे बाहर नहीं, भीतर खोजना है। जो भीतर पाता है, उसे शाश्वत आनन्द मिलता है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'ekaṁ rūpaṁ bahudhā karoti' — this is the divine play (līlā) of one consciousness expressing itself as many forms. 'Ātma-stham' — it is found within, not without. One who finds it within gains eternal ānanda.
aurobindo.ins: The universe is consciousness at play — one actor in a million costumes. The wise person recognises the actor behind every costume and finds joy that nothing can diminish.

dp.q: 🔍 Why is eternal bliss exclusive to the 'wise' (dhīra)?
dp.a: The phrase 'teṣāṁ sukhaṁ śāśvataṁ na itareṣām' — 'eternal bliss is theirs, not others'' — sounds exclusive, but it is descriptive, not prescriptive. It is not that the Self refuses bliss to the unwise — it is that bliss is the natural result of seeing the Self, and its absence is the natural result of not seeing it. An analogy: 'those who open their eyes see the sun; those who keep them shut do not' — this is not cruelty; it is the nature of seeing. The word dhīra (the wise, the steadfast) comes from dhī (intelligence, contemplative understanding). A dhīra is not someone who has memorised scriptures but someone who has developed the inner vision to perceive the Self within. The exclusion 'na itareṣām' is therefore an invitation, not a sentence: become a dhīra, and eternal bliss becomes yours. It is always available — the only barrier is the failure to look.

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'ātma-stham' (established in the Self) mean practically?
dp.a: The compound ātma-stham (ātma + stha = 'standing in the Self') contains a crucial practical teaching: the Self is found within, not without. You do not need to go to a forest, a temple, or a mountain to find the Self — it is 'ātma-stha,' already established in your own being. Practically, this means the path to the Self is introspection, not exploration. The Upanishads describe this as a turning-inward of attention — what the Katha (1.3.12) calls the Self 'hidden in all beings, not manifest, seen by subtle seers with sharp and subtle intellect.' The practice is meditation — specifically, the withdrawal of attention from external objects and its redirection toward the source of awareness itself. 'Who is the one who sees? Who is aware?' — pursuing this question relentlessly leads to the discovery that the seeker IS the sought. The Self is not something you find at the end of a search — it is the one who is searching. To recognise this is to be 'established in the Self' (ātma-stha).

sk: नित्योऽनित्यानां चेतनश्चेतनानाम् एको बहूनां यो विदधाति कामान् | तमात्मस्थं येऽनुपश्यन्ति धीरास्तेषां शान्तिः शाश्वती नेतरेषाम् ||
ro: nityaḥ · anityānāṁ · cetanaḥ · cetanānām · ekaḥ · bahūnāṁ · yaḥ · vidadhāti · kāmān | tam · ātma-sthaṁ · ye · anupaśyanti · dhīrāḥ · teṣāṁ · śāntiḥ · śāśvatī · na · itareṣām ||
hi: अनित्यों में नित्य, चेतनों में (परम) चेतन, जो एक होकर बहुतों की कामनाओं को पूर्ण करता है — जो धीर (बुद्धिमान) उसे आत्मस्थ (अपने आत्मा में स्थित) देखते हैं, उनकी शान्ति शाश्वती (शाश्वत) है — दूसरों की नहीं।
en: The Eternal among the ephemeral, the Conscious among the conscious, the One who fulfils the desires of the many — the wise who see Him established in their own Self, to them belongs eternal peace, and to no others.

ws.e: the Eternal among the non-eternal — nitya (permanent) among anitya (impermanent); the Self alone is changeless amid the changing world
the Conscious among the conscious — cetana (sentient/aware); the Self is the consciousness that makes all other consciousnesses conscious
the One among the many — one Self provides for the many individual souls
fulfils desires — vi + √dhā (to place, to grant); the Self is the ultimate bestower of all that beings desire
eternal peace — śānti (peace) + śāśvatī (perpetual, feminine); not temporary tranquillity but permanent freedom from disturbance
not to others — same exclusion as mantra 12; peace belongs only to those who see the Self

gr: nityaḥ anityānām — 'the Eternal among the non-eternal': a paradox that defines the Self — it is the one unchanging reality amid the ceaseless flux of phenomena. cetanaḥ cetanānām — 'the Conscious among the conscious': not merely conscious but the SOURCE of consciousness in all conscious beings. ekaḥ bahūnāṁ yaḥ vidadhāti kāmān — 'the One who fulfils the desires of the many': the Self, being the substratum of all, is the ultimate provider. śāntiḥ śāśvatī — note the shift from 'sukham' (bliss) in mantra 12 to 'śāntiḥ' (peace) here — deepening the promise: not just bliss (positive) but peace (absence of all disturbance).
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_2.1.13 — This verse is a companion to mantra 12, nearly identical in the second half but with a different first half. The three paradoxical definitions — nitya/anitya, cetana/cetana, eka/bahu — are among the most quoted in Vedāntic literature. This verse also appears in the Shvetashvatara Upanishad (6.13). The shift from 'sukham' to 'śāntiḥ' shows two aspects of liberation: positive bliss AND absence of suffering.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'नित्योऽनित्यानाम्' — ब्रह्म ही एकमात्र नित्य (permanent) तत्त्व है; शेष सब अनित्य (impermanent) है। 'चेतनश्चेतनानाम्' — जीवों की चेतना ब्रह्म की चेतना का प्रतिबिम्ब (reflection) मात्र है। 'शान्ति' — ज्ञान से सब संघर्ष समाप्त होता है; यही शाश्वत शान्ति है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'nityaḥ anityānām' — Brahman alone is the permanent (nitya) reality; everything else is impermanent (anitya). 'Cetanaḥ cetanānām' — the consciousness of beings is merely a reflection of Brahman's consciousness. 'Śānti' — through knowledge all conflict ceases; this is eternal peace.
advaita.ins: You are the eternal among the ephemeral — but you have forgotten. Remember what you are, and the search for peace ends, because you ARE the peace you were seeking.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि 'नित्य' भगवान् हैं, 'अनित्य' जीव और जगत् हैं — पर जीव भी अपने स्वरूप से नित्य हैं, केवल शरीर अनित्य है। 'एकः बहूनां कामान् विदधाति' — भगवान् ही सबकी कामनाओं की पूर्ति करते हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'nitya' is the Lord, 'anitya' are the beings and the world — but beings too are eternal in their essential nature; only the body is impermanent. 'Ekaḥ bahūnāṁ kāmān vidadhāti' — the Lord fulfils the desires of all.
vishisht.ins: The Lord is the one sun from which all moons borrow their light. He is the one consciousness from which all beings draw awareness.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं कि 'नित्योऽनित्यानाम्' — शाश्वत और क्षणिक दो विरोधी (opposites) नहीं हैं; शाश्वत ही क्षणिक के रूप में प्रकट होता है। 'चेतनश्चेतनानाम्' — एक ही चेतना सबमें विविध स्तरों पर प्रकट है। शान्ति — चेतना का अपने मूल स्वरूप में लौटना।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'nityaḥ anityānām' — the eternal and the ephemeral are not two opposites; the eternal manifests AS the ephemeral. 'Cetanaḥ cetanānām' — one consciousness manifests at different levels in all. Peace — is consciousness returning to its original nature.
aurobindo.ins: The eternal does not stand apart from the passing world — it IS the world, seen without the distortion of time. Peace comes when you stop struggling against the flow and recognise yourself as the river, not the leaf upon it.

dp.q: 🔍 What do 'nityaḥ anityānām' and 'cetanaḥ cetanānām' mean?
dp.a: These two phrases are among the most celebrated definitions of the Self in all of Vedānta. 'Nityaḥ anityānām' — 'the Eternal among the non-eternal' — means the Self is the one unchanging reality in a world of ceaseless change. Everything around us — bodies, relationships, civilisations, stars — arises and passes away. But the Self neither arises nor passes away; it is the permanent substrate on which the drama of impermanence plays out. 'Cetanaḥ cetanānām' — 'the Conscious among the conscious' — is even more profound. It does not say 'cetanaḥ acetanānām' (conscious among the unconscious) — it says conscious among the conscious. This means: even the consciousness of sentient beings (humans, animals, gods) is derived from a deeper consciousness — the Self. Your awareness is not self-generated — it is a ray from the Sun of consciousness. The Self is not merely 'another conscious being among many' — it is the source from which all other consciousnesses draw their light.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does the verse shift from 'sukham' (mantra 12) to 'śāntiḥ' (peace)?
dp.a: The shift from sukham (bliss/happiness) in mantra 12 to śāntiḥ (peace) in mantra 13 is deliberate and significant. Sukham is a positive experience — the presence of joy, fulfilment, contentment. Śāntiḥ is the absence of disturbance — no agitation, no craving, no conflict, no fear. Together, they describe two complementary aspects of liberation: (1) You gain something — eternal bliss (sukham śāśvatam); (2) You lose something — all suffering and disturbance (śāntiḥ śāśvatī). The Taittirīya Upanishad (2.7) expresses the positive side: 'raso vai saḥ, rasaṁ hy evāyaṁ labdhvā ānandī bhavati' — 'He is rasa (essence/bliss); having obtained this essence, one becomes blissful.' The triple śānti at the end of every Upanishad prayer (oṁ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ) invokes the negative side: peace from the three sources of suffering — ādhidaivika (cosmic), ādhibhautika (environmental), ādhyātmika (personal). True liberation is both — not just the presence of bliss but the permanent absence of all disturbance.

sk: तदेतदिति मन्यन्तेऽनिर्देश्यं परमं सुखम् | कथं नु तद्विजानीयां किमु भाति विभाति वा ||
ro: tat · etat · iti · manyante · anirdeśyaṁ · paramaṁ · sukham | kathaṁ · nu · tat · vijānīyāṁ · kim · u · bhāti · vibhāti · vā ||
hi: यह वह है — ऐसा (ज्ञानी) मानते हैं — वह अनिर्देश्य (अवर्णनीय), परम सुख। मैं उसे कैसे जानूँ? क्या वह (स्वयं) प्रकाशित है, या (किसी अन्य से) प्रकाशमान होता है?
en: 'This is That' — so they recognise the indescribable, supreme bliss. How then may I know it? Does it shine (of its own light), or does it shine (by reflected light)?

ws.e: indescribable — a (not) + nirdeśya (that which can be pointed out/described); Brahman cannot be captured in words
