supreme bliss — parama (highest) + sukha (happiness); not any ordinary pleasure but the ultimate fulfilment
how — the seeker's question: by what means can this be known?
may I know — optative first person singular of vi + √jñā; expressing earnest aspiration to know
does it shine — √bhā (to shine); does Brahman shine by its own light?
does it shine forth / does it shine differently — vi + √bhā; an alternative reading: does it shine reflected/variously?

gr: tat etat iti manyante — 'they think: this is That' — the wise recognise Brahman as 'this' (etat, the immediate experience) being identical with 'that' (tat, the ultimate reality). anirdeśyam — 'indescribable': Brahman cannot be pointed to, named, or defined in ordinary language. kathaṁ nu tat vijānīyām — 'how may I know That?' — a question within the teaching, expressing the paradox of knowing the unknowable. kim u bhāti vibhāti vā — 'does it shine or does it shine variously?': the question is about the source of Brahman's luminosity — is it self-luminous or illuminated by something else? The answer follows in mantra 15.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_2.1.14 — This verse poses the epistemological question: how can the indescribable be known? The question 'kim u bhāti vibhāti vā' sets up the magnificent answer in mantra 15 about Brahman's self-luminosity. The phrase 'anirdeśyam' echoes the Taittirīya (2.4): 'yato vāco nivartante aprāpya manasā saha' — 'from which words return, together with the mind, unable to reach it.'

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि 'अनिर्देश्य' — ब्रह्म शब्दों से वर्णनीय नहीं, क्योंकि शब्द विशेषणों (attributes) के माध्यम से कार्य करते हैं, और ब्रह्म निर्विशेष (without attributes) है। 'कथं विजानीयाम्?' — यह प्रश्न स्वयं उत्तर का मार्ग है: ब्रह्म को जानने का माध्यम 'नेति नेति' (not this, not this) है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'anirdeśya' — Brahman cannot be described in words because words operate through attributes (viśeṣaṇas), and Brahman is attributeless (nirviśeṣa). 'How may I know it?' — this question itself is the path to the answer: Brahman is known through 'neti neti' (not this, not this).
advaita.ins: You cannot describe Brahman in words — but you can recognise it when every description has been negated. What remains when you have said 'not this' to everything — that is Brahman.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि 'अनिर्देश्य' — भगवान् सामान्य वाणी से नहीं, पर वेद और भक्ति से ज्ञात हो सकते हैं। 'कथं विजानीयाम्?' — भक्ति, शरणागति, और गुरुकृपा के माध्यम से। भगवान् स्वयं अपने भक्त को ज्ञान प्रदान करते हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'anirdeśya' — the Lord cannot be known through ordinary speech, but can be known through scripture and devotion. 'How may I know it?' — through bhakti, surrender, and the guru's grace. The Lord Himself grants knowledge to His devotee.
vishisht.ins: The Lord is beyond description but not beyond love. The mind cannot grasp Him, but the heart can reach Him.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं कि 'अनिर्देश्य' — ब्रह्म मन और वाणी से परे है, पर चेतना के गहनतम स्तर पर सीधे अनुभव-योग्य (directly experienceable) है। 'किम् उ भाति विभाति वा' — यह प्रश्न चेतना की प्रकृति के बारे में है: क्या चेतना स्व-प्रकाश है?
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'anirdeśya' — Brahman is beyond mind and speech, but directly experienceable at the deepest level of consciousness. 'Kim u bhāti vibhāti vā' — this question is about the nature of consciousness: is consciousness self-luminous?
aurobindo.ins: The supreme reality is not something you can think about — it is something you become. The question 'how to know it?' dissolves when you realise you ARE it.

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'anirdeśya' (indescribable) mean for spiritual knowledge?
dp.a: The term anirdeśya (a + nirdeśya = 'that which cannot be pointed out or described') is one of the most important epistemological terms in the Upanishads. It does not mean that Brahman is unknowable — it means Brahman is unknowable by the ordinary means of knowledge (perception, inference, and verbal testimony as normally understood). Words work by distinguishing one thing from another — 'the cow is not a horse.' But Brahman, being all-inclusive, cannot be distinguished from anything, because there is nothing outside it. You cannot say 'Brahman is X' without implying 'Brahman is not Y' — but Brahman is also Y. The Taittirīya (2.4) captures this: 'yato vāco nivartante aprāpya manasā saha' — 'From which words turn back, together with the mind, unable to reach.' Yet the Upanishads do teach about Brahman — through negation (neti neti — 'not this, not this'), through analogy (fire, wind, sun), through paradox (smaller than the smallest, greater than the greatest), and through direct pointing (tat tvam asi — 'You are That'). The word anirdeśya is itself a description — a finger pointing beyond all fingers.

dp.q: 🔍 What is the question 'does it shine or does it shine forth'?
dp.a: The question 'kim u bhāti vibhāti vā' asks whether Brahman is self-luminous (svayaṁ-prakāśa) or illuminated by something else (para-prakāśa). This is a foundational question in epistemology. If Brahman shines by its own light — it needs no external source and is therefore the ultimate reality. If it is illuminated by something else — then that 'something else' would be the ultimate reality. The answer comes in the next verse (mantra 15): 'na tatra sūryo bhāti na candra-tārakaṁ' — 'The sun does not shine there, nor the moon, nor the stars.' Brahman is the light by which all other lights shine. The sun does not illuminate Brahman; Brahman illuminates the sun. This is the doctrine of svayaṁ-prakāśatva (self-luminosity) — consciousness is not revealed by anything else; it is the revealer of all things. You see objects by the light of the sun; you see the sun by the light of consciousness. But you do not see consciousness by any light — consciousness IS the light.

sk: न तत्र सूर्यो भाति न चन्द्रतारकं नेमा विद्युतो भान्ति कुतोऽयमग्निः | तमेव भान्तमनुभाति सर्वं तस्य भासा सर्वमिदं विभाति ||
ro: na · tatra · sūryaḥ · bhāti · na · candra-tārakaṁ · na · imāḥ · vidyutaḥ · bhānti · kutaḥ · ayam · agniḥ | tam · eva · bhāntam · anubhāti · sarvaṁ · tasya · bhāsā · sarvam · idaṁ · vibhāti ||
hi: वहाँ (ब्रह्म में) न सूर्य प्रकाशित होता है, न चन्द्र और तारे, न ये विद्युत् (बिजली) चमकती हैं — तो यह अग्नि (सांसारिक अग्नि) कहाँ से (चमक सकती है)? उसी के प्रकाशित होने पर सब कुछ अनुप्रकाशित (प्रकाशित) होता है; उसकी ज्योति से यह सब विभाति (चमकता) है।
en: The sun does not shine there, nor the moon and stars, nor these lightnings — how then this (ordinary) fire? Him alone shining, everything shines after; by His light, all this shines forth.

ws.s: न तत्र सूर्यः भाति (na tatra sūryaḥ bhāti)
ws.e: the sun does not shine there — tatra: in that (Brahman); the sun's light is derivative, not original
nor the moon and stars — the greatest celestial lights are dim before Brahman
nor these lightnings — even the most dramatic natural light cannot illuminate Brahman
how then this fire? — a rhetorical escalation: if sun/moon/lightning can't shine there, what chance has ordinary fire?

ws.s: तम् एव भान्तम् अनुभाति सर्वम् (tam eva bhāntam anubhāti sarvam)
ws.h: उसी के चमकने पर सब कुछ चमकता है
ws.e: Him alone shining, everything shines after — anubhāti: shines after (anu = following); all light is derivative of Brahman's light
by His light — bhāsā: instrumental of bhās (light/lustre); Brahman's light is the source of all illumination

gr: na tatra sūryaḥ bhāti — 'the sun does not shine there': this does not mean the sun literally goes dark in the presence of Brahman — it means the sun's capacity to illuminate is itself derived from Brahman. The sun is a secondary light, not a primary one. kutaḥ ayam agniḥ — a rhetorical climax: if even the sun, moon, stars, and lightning cannot illuminate Brahman, how can ordinary fire? tam eva bhāntam anubhāti sarvam — 'everything shines AFTER Him alone shining': the key word is anu (after/following) — all light follows from and depends on Brahman's self-luminosity. tasya bhāsā sarvam idaṁ vibhāti — 'by His light all this shines': the conclusive statement — Brahman is the ultimate source of all light, physical and conscious.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: katha_upanishad_2.1.15 — One of the most celebrated verses in all of Indian philosophy. It appears nearly identically in the Mundaka Upanishad (2.2.10), the Shvetashvatara Upanishad (6.14), and is echoed in the Bhagavad Gītā (15.6 and 15.12). This verse answers the question of mantra 14 ('does it shine?') with a resounding declaration of Brahman's absolute self-luminosity. It also establishes the Vedāntic doctrine that consciousness is the primary light from which all physical light derives.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं कि यह मन्त्र ब्रह्म की स्वयंप्रकाशता (self-luminosity) सिद्ध करता है। सूर्य भी ब्रह्म की ज्योति से प्रकाशित है — जैसे लोहा अग्नि से तप्त होकर चमकता है, पर चमक लोहे की नहीं, अग्नि की है। वैसे ही सूर्य की चमक ब्रह्म की है।
advaita.en: Shankara says this verse establishes Brahman's self-luminosity (svayaṁ-prakāśatva). Even the sun is illuminated by Brahman's light — as iron heated by fire glows, but the glow belongs to the fire, not the iron. So the sun's radiance belongs to Brahman.
advaita.ins: The sun lights the world, but what lights the sun? Consciousness lights the sun. Without a conscious being to perceive it, the sun's light illuminates nothing. Brahman is the light behind all lights.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं कि भगवान् स्वयं-ज्योतिः (self-luminous) हैं — सूर्य, चन्द्र, अग्नि — ये सब भगवान् की तेजस्विता के अंश हैं। भगवान् का परमधाम (Vaikuṇṭha) भौतिक प्रकाश से नहीं, भगवान् के अपने तेज से प्रकाशित होता है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the Lord is self-luminous (svayaṁ-jyotiḥ) — sun, moon, fire — all are portions of the Lord's radiance. The Lord's supreme abode (Vaikuṇṭha) is illuminated not by physical light but by the Lord's own effulgence.
vishisht.ins: In the Lord's abode, there is no need for sun or moon — the Lord Himself is the light. This is not poetic metaphor; it is the nature of divine reality.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं कि यह मन्त्र चेतना (consciousness) को प्रकाश का मूल स्रोत (ultimate source of light) घोषित करता है। भौतिक प्रकाश (सूर्य, अग्नि) चेतना के प्रकाश का एक बाह्य अभिव्यक्ति मात्र है। चेतना पहले है; भौतिक प्रकाश बाद में।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says this verse declares consciousness as the ultimate source of light. Physical light (sun, fire) is merely an external expression of the light of consciousness. Consciousness comes first; physical light comes after.
aurobindo.ins: All light — from the sun's blaze to the glow of a firefly — is an echo of one original light: consciousness. When you see anything at all, you are witnessing the Self's self-luminosity reflected through matter.

dp.q: 🔍 Why can't the sun, moon, or fire illuminate Brahman?
dp.a: This verse makes a radical claim: the greatest sources of physical light — sun, moon, stars, lightning, fire — cannot illuminate Brahman. This is because all these lights are secondary — they derive their capacity to illuminate from Brahman itself. Consider: the sun illuminates objects, making them visible. But what makes the sun itself 'visible'? It is consciousness — without a conscious observer, the sun illuminates nothing. The sun does not know it shines; only a conscious being knows the sun shines. Therefore consciousness (= Brahman) is the prior light that makes all other lights meaningful. This is the doctrine of svayaṁ-prakāśatva: consciousness is self-luminous — it reveals itself by itself, without needing any external light to reveal it. You know you are conscious — but by what light do you know this? Not by the sun's light; not by any physical light. Consciousness knows itself by its own light. This makes it the ultimate source of all illumination.

dp.q: 🔍 How does this verse appear across different scriptures?
dp.a: This verse — or near-identical versions of it — appears in at least four major texts, making it one of the most frequently quoted verses in the entire Hindu scriptural tradition. (1) Katha Upanishad 2.1.15 — the version here. (2) Mundaka Upanishad 2.2.10 — virtually identical: 'na tatra sūryo bhāti na candra-tārakaṁ nemā vidyuto bhānti kuto'yam agniḥ.' (3) Shvetashvatara Upanishad 6.14 — same content with minor variations. (4) Bhagavad Gītā 15.6: 'na tad bhāsayate sūryo na śaśāṅko na pāvakaḥ; yad gatvā na nivartante tad dhāma paramaṁ mama' — 'Neither sun nor moon nor fire illuminates that; having gone there, one does not return — that is My supreme abode.' And Gītā 15.12: 'yad āditya-gataṁ tejo jagad bhāsayate'khilam' — 'The light in the sun that illuminates the whole world — know that light to be Mine.' This widespread repetition shows the verse was considered one of the most essential declarations about the nature of the Absolute across the Upanishadic and post-Upanishadic traditions.
